description: We're a two-person team building a 3D interactive Moon explorer for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. I'm a full-stack developer and startup founder handling the core engineering and interactive build, and my friend brings the space science background to handle the data and landing site analysis.
summary:
Apollo Mission is a playable 3D simulation where students plan and fly their own Apollo 11 mission on real NASA data. In a planner built on NASA JPL Horizons, they pick:

a launch date
any landing point on the Moon
the lunar module’s fuel load
a free-return or hybrid route

A flight director’s GO / NO-GO poll checks every choice against real Apollo rules, including the real weather at Kennedy from NASA POWER records.

Then they fly it:

launch from Pad 39A inside the Smithsonian’s 3D scan of the real Apollo 11 command module
docking with the lunar module
a hand-flown course correction
the burn that puts them in orbit behind the Moon
a landing at their chosen point on terrain built from NASA LOLA heights, with the real 1969 radio

Seven real Apollo emergencies are triggered by the player’s own choices, among them Apollo 11’s 1202 alarm, Apollo 12’s lightning strike, Apollo 13’s engine failure and Apollo 14’s fake abort signal. Wrong decisions are played out, explained in plain language and rewound, and there are no scores. By turning real mission-design trade-offs into decisions students make and live with, it teaches spaceflight the way mission planners learned it.
details:
Apollo Mission lets you design and fly Apollo 11 from launch day to touchdown.

  1. Planning: on a to-scale Earth and Moon placed with NASA JPL Horizons data for any day from 2026 to 2028, you choose:
    The weather at the pad comes from real NASA POWER daily records for Kennedy Space Center. A flight director’s GO / NO-GO poll checks the flight path, the rocket, life support and the weather.
    • Launch date and landing site: any point on the Moon. The site needs the Sun 5–14° up and rising, with Earth in view for radio.
    • The lunar module’s fuel: more hover time at the landing, but less spare performance for the Saturn V.
    • The route: free return is safe but only reaches sites near the Moon’s centre; hybrid reaches any site.
  2. Launch: from LC-39A, from inside the real Apollo 11 command module (a Smithsonian 3D scan). The climb replays the real Saturn V trajectory with the original air-to-ground radio.
  3. The trip: you dock with the lunar module yourself, fire the course correction by hand, and press PRO for the burn behind the Moon.
  4. The landing: at the exact coordinates you chose. The terrain comes from NASA LOLA elevation and the LROC colour map, with craters and boulders generated where the data is too coarse. As on Apollo 11, the computer aims at a crater full of boulders, and you fly the last 150 m by hand while the fuel runs out.

Benefits and impact

  • Students don’t memorize facts; they make the decisions real mission planners made, such as launch windows, landing-site lighting, fuel margins and abort choices.
  • Every problem is real: the 1202 alarm, Apollo 12’s lightning, Apollo 13’s engine failure, Apollo 14’s docking latches, radar and solder ball, and Apollo 12’s dust. Each is caused by the player’s own choices, for example launching into rain clouds or leaving a radar switch on.
  • A mistake is shown, explained in simple words, and rewound, so failure becomes the lesson.
  • Every run differs, because the date, the site, the real weather and your choices change the light, the terrain and the problems.

Tools and languages

  • Unity 2022.3 LTS with the Universal Render Pipeline
    • a volumetric cloud renderer
    • a single-scattering atmosphere
    • lunar terrain with shadows ray-marched toward the low Sun
  • Python (NumPy, Pillow) to convert the NASA data
  • Built and tested on an ordinary laptop with integrated Intel Iris Xe graphics, so schools can run it.

How it is creative

  • The real 1969 radio plays at the matching moments; we located each line in the recordings.
  • Weather drives the story: rain clouds cause the lightning strike, as they did for Apollo 12.
  • You land at the exact place you clicked on the Moon, on real elevation data.
  • The game shows you what would have happened, and the rewind lets you try the decision again.

What we considered

  • Historical accuracy: real Apollo timelines, numbers, launch rules and fixes, checked against the Apollo Flight Journal and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal.
  • Clear, minimal design for students.
  • Pacing: the 8-day mission takes about 5 minutes of play.
  • Running on low-end hardware.
  • No scores, so students learn from what happened instead of chasing points.
dataRefs: NASA JPL Horizons (Earth, Moon and Sun positions)
NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit (LROC color map, LOLA elevation)
NASA POWER daily weather, Kennedy Space Center 1981-2025
Apollo Flight Journal (Apollo 11 and 12 audio, timelines)
Apollo Lunar Surface Journal (Apollo 11 and 14 landing audio, transcripts)
NASA Technical Reports Server (Saturn V AS-506 trajectory, Apollo 11 Mission Report)
